scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

### Quick‑Start Guide to Getting Hongbao Ready for Your Cousins | Step | What to Do | Why It Helps | Tips & Tricks | |------|------------|--------------|---------------| | **1. Decide on the Amount** | Think about age, relationship, and your budget. | A thoughtful amount shows respect without breaking the bank. | • **Kids (5‑10 yr)**: ¥5‑¥20 (or the equivalent in your local currency).
• **Teens (11‑18 yr)**: ¥20‑¥50.
• **Older teens/young adults**: ¥50‑¥200.
• Use “lucky numbers” (8, 6, 9) for extra good‑fortune vibes. | | **2. Choose Your Red Envelopes** | Grab a pack of red envelopes (红包) from a nearby Asian market, online store, or even a DIY set. | Red is the traditional color for luck and prosperity. | • Look for envelopes with **gold characters** (“福”, “恭喜发财”).
• If you’re short on time, plain red envelopes are fine—just write a quick blessing. | | **3. Write a Simple Blessing** | Inside or on the front, add a short phrase. | It personalizes the gift and adds cultural meaning. | • “恭喜发财” (Gōngxǐ fācái) – “Wishing you wealth.”
• “万事如意” (Wànshì rúyì) – “May all your wishes come true.”
• For kids, “健康成长” (Jiànkāng chéngzhǎng) – “Healthy growth.” | | **4. Add a Personal Touch (Optional)** | Slip a tiny note, a sticker, or a small doodle. | Shows you put extra effort, which kids love. | • A tiny cartoon of a **golden pig** (Year of the Pig) or **dragon**.
• A mini‑photo of you together. | | **5. Pack Efficiently** | If you have many cousins, group envelopes in a small box or decorative bag. | Keeps everything tidy and makes distribution smoother. | • Use a **gift box** lined with red tissue paper.
• Add a ribbon for a festive look. | | **6. Consider Digital Hongbao** | If you’re really pressed for time, many apps let you send e‑hongbao instantly. | No need to print or travel; the money arrives instantly. | • **WeChat Pay** “红包” feature.
• **Alipay** “红包”.
• Some Western apps (e.g., PayPal, Venmo) let you send a “gift” with a custom note—just add a red‑themed image. | | **7. Timing** | Hand out the envelopes **right after the New Year’s Eve dinner** or when you first see the cousins on New Year’s Day. | Tradition says the first encounter of the year should be lucky. | • If you’re meeting later in the day, still give them before the **first meal** you share. | | **8. Follow Up** | After they open the hongbao, wish them “新年快乐!” (Xīnnián kuàilè) – “Happy New Year!” | Reinforces the festive spirit. | • A quick selfie together makes a great memory for later sharing. | --- ## Speed‑Run Options (If You’re Really in a Hurry) 1. **Buy Pre‑Made Sets** – Many supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Target, Asian grocery chains) sell ready‑filled red envelopes with cash already inside. Grab a pack, add a quick handwritten note, and you’re done. 2. **DIY on Paper** – Cut small red squares (about 8 cm × 8 cm), fold them into mini‑envelopes, and tape the edges. It looks cute and can be done in minutes. 3. **Digital First, Physical Later** – Send a digital hongbao today, then mail a small physical envelope later in the week as a “follow‑up surprise.” This covers both immediacy and tradition. --- ## Cultural Quick‑Facts (In Case You Want to Impress) | Fact | Explanation | |------|--------------| | **Red = Luck** | Red wards off evil spirits and attracts good fortune. | | **Even Numbers** | Even numbers (especially 8) are considered auspicious; avoid odd numbers like 4 (which sounds like “death”). | | **Avoid “4”** | The Mandarin word for four (四, *sì*) sounds like “death” (死, *sǐ*). If possible, skip amounts ending in 4. | | **Give New Money** | Use brand‑new bills (not old or torn ones) to symbolize fresh beginnings. | | **No “Empty” Envelopes** | Make sure the envelope is sealed and the cash is visible; an empty envelope is considered bad luck. | --- ### Sample Script When Handing Out the Hongbao > **You:** “恭喜发财! 新年快乐! 这是给你的红包，祝你在新的一年里学习进步、健康快乐！” > **Translation:** “Congratulations and may you prosper! Happy New Year! Here’s a red envelope for you—wishing you progress in school and good health this year!” --- ## TL;DR Checklist - [ ] Pick amount (use lucky numbers). - [ ] Grab red envelopes (store‑bought or DIY). - [ ] Write a short blessing. - [ ] Add a tiny personal note or sticker (optional). - [ ] Pack them nicely or send digitally. - [ ] Hand them out right after the New Year’s celebration. - [ ] Wish “新年快乐!” and enjoy the smiles. You’ve got this! Even if you start a day or two late, the gesture of giving hongbao is what truly matters. Happy Chūnjié! 🎉🧧✨
